Respiratory Illness Outbreak in 2021 Disrupted Japanese Steel Industry

In a significant incident that unfolded in early 2021, a sudden outbreak of acute respiratory illness swept through several steel manufacturing sites across western Japan, temporarily disrupting operations and highlighting vulnerabilities in the industry’s health protocols.

Sanyo Special Steel Co Ltd, a major player based in Hyogo Prefecture, confirmed that nearly 60 employees at its main plant reported symptoms consistent with viral pneumonia over the course of three weeks in February 2021. Local health authorities later identified the cause as a cluster of adenovirus infections, a common but potentially serious illness in crowded industrial settings.

Operations at Sanyo Special Steel Co Ltd’s works were suspended for five days while thorough disinfection and contact tracing were undertaken. Production lines at other companies, including the Kobe-based Hinode Steelworks, also slowed as hundreds of workers across the region reported sick leave. Industry analysts estimate that steel output in western Japan fell by approximately 4% during the first quarter of 2021 as a direct result of the outbreak. 

“The health and safety of our employees is our top priority,” said a spokesperson for Sanyo Special Steel Co Ltd in a statement released at the time. “We worked closely with local health officials to contain the spread and ensure a safe return to work for our staff.”

Union representatives noted that the outbreak exposed gaps in health monitoring and preventative measures at large industrial sites, where staff often work in close quarters. “This was a wake-up call for the whole sector,” said Masaru Tanaka, a spokesperson for the Hyogo Workers’ Union. “We have since pushed for stricter health checks and better ventilation in the plants.”

The Japan Iron and Steel Federation issued guidance following the incident, recommending enhanced screening and hygiene protocols. “The temporary decrease in output was challenging,” an industry analyst, Keiko Ueno, commented. “But the swift response averted a more severe impact and led to improved practices that continue to benefit the workforce.”

By late March 2021, affected plants—including those of Sanyo Special Steel Co Ltd—had resumed normal operations. No further disruptions have been reported since, and the measures adopted during the outbreak are now considered a benchmark for industrial health management in the region.
